speaker: Eric Jang
title: What rebuilding AlphaGo teaches us about self-play, RL, and future of LLMs - Eric Jang
question: Why do early frontier AI and robotics training runs often sit far off the compute-optimal scaling curve?
guest: Being the first to do something means you are prioritizing getting the thing working rather than building the most compute-efficient possible implementation. This actually plays out in robotics as well. If you look at the frontier of large models trained for robotics, the scatter plot is all over the place, and there is not a clean line the way there is for frontier LLMs. That is because the teams training these models are often not yet at the scale where every FLOP counts and they need to squeeze maximum performance out of every single FLOP as the deciding factor in training. Instead, their focus is wanting a certain capability to show up, so they optimize the training setup to make it easy to derive that capability. Once you have that capability, invariably when you scale up compute, you are forced to make it compute-efficient because you are talking about hundreds of millions of dollars. When experiment compute is more plentiful or not accounted for at that scale, people optimize for things besides sitting on the compute-optimal Pareto frontier.

points.core: First-mover teams prioritize unlocking a new capability over squeezing FLOP efficiency.
points.note: Accept: pioneers optimize for getting a capability to work or time-to-result rather than sitting on the compute-optimal Pareto frontier. Do not credit: claiming early teams simply lacked engineering skill.

points.core: Early robotics runs operate below the budget scale where FLOPs dominate.
points.note: Accept: smaller compute budgets or unbilled research compute mean every FLOP is not yet the binding constraint, explaining noisy robotics scaling scatter plots. Do not credit: generic claims that robotics data is hard.

points.core: Extreme training costs later force teams onto the compute-optimal frontier.
points.note: Accept: scaling a proven capability to hundred-million-dollar budgets financially forces teams to optimize FLOP efficiency. Do not credit: vague statements that hardware gets cheaper over time.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Early frontier runs usually sit off the compute-optimal curve because the optimal curve isn't known in advance and the binding constraint is rarely compute alone.

Compute-optimal scaling (as in the Chinchilla analysis) says that for a given compute budget there is a best ratio of model size to training data. But that ratio has to be discovered empirically through expensive sweeps, and the first groups at a new scale are extrapolating from smaller regimes. GPT-3-era language models, for example, turned out to be substantially oversized and undertrained on tokens relative to what later analysis showed was optimal.

The second reason is data scarcity. In robotics especially, high-quality demonstration or interaction data is costly and slow to collect, so teams cannot simply add data to match a larger model. They end up data-limited rather than compute-limited, training models that are too large for their datasets or leaning on pretrained backbones, simulation, and augmentation.

Finally, early runs optimize for other things: proving capability quickly, reusing existing architectures and hardware, limiting inference cost, or hedging against training instability, rather than squeezing maximum loss reduction per FLOP.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Compute-optimal scaling laws minimize pretraining FLOPs for a target loss assuming abundant data and tuned hyperparameters—conditions rarely met in early frontier AI or robotics. First, the curve itself is initially unknown: early language model runs like GPT-3 followed biased fixed-schedule extrapolations that produced oversized, undertrained models before Chinchilla revised the parameter-to-token ratio, while nascent robotics architectures still lack settled scaling exponents across multimodal sensorimotor inputs. Second, data bottlenecks force deviations, especially in robotics, where collecting real-world demonstrations is slow and expensive; teams must train for many epochs on limited trajectories or graft action heads onto pretrained vision-language backbones rather than scaling fresh data alongside parameters. Third, training optimality ignores deployment realities: frontier labs deliberately overtrain smaller models to cut inference costs, and robots require compact weights to satisfy strict onboard compute and real-time control latency budgets. Finally, early runs prioritize wall-clock iteration speed and cluster utilization over raw FLOP efficiency, choosing large batch sizes and hardware-friendly model shapes that accelerate debugging and reduce engineering risk.

noweb.answer:
Early frontier AI and robotics training runs frequently diverge from compute-optimal scaling curves because theoretical training FLOP efficiency rarely aligns with real-world data, deployment, and systems constraints. Compute-optimal laws assume abundant data and well-characterized loss surfaces, yet early runs in novel architectures or modalities take place before scaling exponents and hyperparameter transfer rules are empirically established. Data bottlenecks make this especially acute in robotics, where real-world interaction and teleoperation trajectories are scarce and expensive to collect, forcing teams to lean on pretrained backbones, over-parameterize models, or repeat epochs rather than scaling fresh data proportionally.

Furthermore, training-optimal curves ignore inference constraints and hardware realities. Robotics demands low-latency, high-frequency control on limited onboard compute, while frontier AI labs optimize for long-term serving economics—leading both fields to deliberately overtrain smaller models well past their training-optimal point. Finally, cluster topologies, memory bandwidth limits, and strict wall-clock deadlines push engineers toward model shapes and batch sizes that maximize accelerator utilization and research iteration speed rather than pure FLOP optimality.

quotes: strict wall-clock deadlines push engineers toward model shapes and batch sizes that maximize accelerator utilization and research iteration speed rather than pure FLOP optimality.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Early frontier AI and robotics runs usually sit far off the compute-optimal curve because the curve isn't known yet, and because "optimal" there means something narrower than what teams are actually optimizing for.

First, scaling laws have to be measured before anyone can follow them. That takes many careful sweeps, which new domains don't have. Early estimates can also be wrong: GPT-3 and Gopher were undertrained partly because Kaplan's 2020 fits used learning-rate schedules that weren't tuned to each run's length. Chinchilla later corrected this.

Second, data is often the real bottleneck. Robot trajectories are scarce, expensive and slow to collect, so teams can't grow data to match compute. They end up repeating data or using oversized models instead.

Third, compute-optimal only means the lowest pretraining loss for a fixed training budget. Real projects care about other things too. They deliberately overtrain smaller models to cut inference costs, as Llama did, or to meet latency and memory limits on robot hardware. They also judge success by downstream skills rather than loss.

Finally, early infrastructure is immature. Low hardware utilization, instabilities, untuned hyperparameters and deadlines push runs off the ideal frontier.

points.why: The candidate mentions downstream skills as a success metric but never says first movers trade FLOP efficiency for getting a new capability to work.
The candidate identifies scarce robot trajectories as a bottleneck and leaves unexplained why FLOP efficiency is not yet a binding budget constraint.
The candidate leaves out the financial pressure to improve FLOP efficiency when scaling a proven capability to very large training budgets.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Early frontier AI and robotics training runs often sit far off the compute-optimal scaling curve because teams are operating before the true scaling laws, data regimes, and architectures for a new domain are understood. Compute-optimal training requires balancing model size, dataset size, and hyperparameters precisely, yet early efforts rely on rough heuristics—often over-allocating parameters relative to data, as seen in pre-Chinchilla language models, or using suboptimal learning-rate schedules and batch sizes. In robotics especially, data scarcity is a major bottleneck: collecting diverse, high-quality real-world trajectories is slow and expensive, leaving large vision-language-action models severely data-constrained compared to text models. Early runs also suffer from immature architectures, inefficient tokenization or action representations, training instabilities, and low hardware utilization from untested distributed infrastructure. Finally, teams sometimes deliberately depart from compute-optimal points to satisfy downstream constraints—such as overtraining smaller models for fast, low-latency inference on robot hardware—or simply to prove a new capability exists before optimizing for efficiency.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A compute-optimal scaling curve estimates how to split a training budget between model size and data to get the lowest loss for a given training setup. Early frontier runs often happen before teams know that relationship reliably. They may choose a large model to test whether a capability appears, reuse a fixed dataset to compare methods, or pick a configuration that fits their hardware and deadline. Those choices can make a run more informative or easier to execute while sacrificing some loss improvement per FLOP.

Robotics adds a bottleneck that extra compute alone can’t remove. Real-world experience takes time to collect, robots need resets and supervision, and simulated experience may transfer imperfectly. A team can have spare accelerator capacity and still be short of useful training data. The run is shaped by what the team needs to learn and which resources are scarce.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A compute-optimal scaling curve describes how to spend a fixed training budget to get the best result, given a particular model, dataset, and objective. Early runs often serve a different purpose. A team may train a large model briefly to learn whether a new capability appears or whether its training setup works at scale. That can guide the next experiment even if a smaller model trained longer would achieve lower loss for the same compute.

Teams also have to estimate the curve from earlier experiments, and those estimates may transfer poorly to a new architecture or task. In robotics, compute can be available long before enough diverse, high-quality robot experience has been collected. Replaying the same trajectories buys less new information, while collecting fresh ones takes physical time. The gap can therefore reflect a deliberate trade-off, uncertainty about the optimum, or a data bottleneck.
